IN THE SUPREME COURT OF
BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:                       )

MEDICAL SERVICES COMMISSION  )   MADAM
JUSTICE ROWLES

Counsel for the petitioner:                    John
J. Steeves

Counsel for the respondents:                     Paul
Pearlman

Place and Date of Hearing:         Vancouver,
British Columbia

June
l0 & ll, l99l

The Petitioner, Timothy Knodel,
seeks a declaration pursuant to s. 2(2) of the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 209, that the Respondents, their agents or servants have by
way of a letter decision of September l, l988, misinterpreted the definition of
"spouse" in s. 2.01 of the
Medical Service Act Regulations
,
B.C. Reg. 144/68 ("
Regulations"
), made pursuant to the
provisions of the
Medical Service Act
, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 255, by
attributing to the definition an interpretation contrary to the provisions of
s.l5(l) of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, Part l of the
Constitution
Act, l982
.

"Spouse" is defined in
the
Regulations
as follows:

"spouse"
includes a man or woman who, not being married to each other, live together as
husband and wife.

The impugned interpretation of
the definition of "spouse" was contained in a letter sent on behalf
of the Respondent Medical Services Commission, which denied medical coverage to
the Petitioner's same sex-life partner, Ray Garneau, as a dependent spouse
under the Petitioner's medical services plan coverage.  The letter stated, in
part:

Our legal counsel has
confirmed that the Medical Service Act Regulations' definition of `spouse' is
interpreted to mean a wife, in relation to a male subscriber; or a husband, in
relation to a female subscriber.  The Medical Services Plan of British Columbia
recognizes both legal marriages and common-law relationships, but only those of
a heterosexual nature.

Alternatively, in the event that
the definition of "spouse" is found not to include same-sex couples,
the Petitioner seeks a declaration that s. 2.01 of the
Regulations

infringes his right to equality pursuant to
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.  In
that event, the Petitioner says that an appropriate and just remedy pursuant to

s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
is to "read in" the inclusion of
homosexual couples into the definition of "spouse" in the
Regulations
.

The Respondents' position is that
the
Regulations
, and specifically, the definition of spouse, has not
inflicted any disadvantage, or had any adverse impact upon the Petitioner, and
that accordingly, the legislative impact of the
Regulations
, as applied
to the Petitioner, has not been discriminatory and there has been no violation
of the Petitioner's equality rights under s.l5(l) of the
Charter
.
Further, the Respondents' position is that s.l5(l) of the
Charter

prohibits discrimination, but does not forbid the making of distinctions, and
that in this case, there is a distinction, not based on sexual orientation, but
rather on a distinction between "spouses" and the wider class of
"non-spouses" who do not hold themselves out as man and wife, but who
may live in the same household unit, such as brother/sister, or parent/adult
child, and do not enjoy the benefit, even though one may be financially
dependent on the other.

The Proceedings

The Petition was filed on
December 22, l989.  On July l0, l990, Mr. Justice Low granted, by consent, the
Petitioner's application to hold a trial of the proceedings, and ordered that
pleadings be filed.  A Statement of Claim and Statement of Defence were filed.
When the trial came before me, the evidence consisted of affidavits and an
expert report.

The Statement of Defence alleged
that the plaintiff (Petitioner) had not followed the appeal procedure set out
in the
Regulations
, but by agreement between counsel, the issue of
whether or not the Plaintiff was required to exhaust all his remedies under the

Regulations
before coming to court was not advanced by the defendants
(Respondents) as a bar to the court granting relief.

The Parties

The Petitioner is a licensed
practical nurse at the University Hospital, Shaughnessy Site ("Hospital"),
in Vancouver, and is a member of the Hospital Employees's Union
("Union") which is the sole bargaining agent for 35,000 hospital
employees in British Columbia.

The Respondent Medical Services
Commission ("Commission") is duly constituted pursuant to s. 2 of the

Medical Service Act
, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 209 ("
MSA
").
The Commission is empowered under s. 7 of the
MSA
to administer and
operate the Medical Services Plan ("Plan").  The Plan, established
pursuant to s. 9 of the
MSA
, is a voluntary medical plan for the
provision of medical insurance and licensing of carriers that provide medical
insurance in the Province.  Pursuant to the
Act
and the
Regulations
,
eligible persons who pay the premiums established by the Plan are entitled to
receive the insured health care services defined in the legislation.

The Respondent Christopher
Henderson is a Commissioner and the Chairman of the Commission.  He is
appointed pursuant to s. 2(2) of the
MSA
and is responsible for the
administration of the
MSA
.

Background

The following background is taken
from affidavits filed by the Petitioner, which are not in dispute.

The Petitioner was involved in a
live-in monogamous homosexual relationship with Ray Garneau from May 27, 1984,
until Mr. Garneau's death on March 17, 1989.  Mr. Garneau was also employed a
licensed Practical Nurse at the Hospital from 1987 to 1988.

The Petitioner and Mr. Garneau
agreed to live together and offered each other financial, emotional and moral
support. They exchanged wedding bands to symbolize their love and commitment
towards each other.  Their relationship was both known and supported by their
family members and friends.  Mr. Garneau's parents gave them a vacation in Reno
as a gift in 1988.  They took vacations together whenever they could.  In 1985,
they drove to the United States on a four day trip.  In 1986, they visited Mr.
Garneau's parents in Vancouver Island, visited Long Beach and visited the
Petitioner's parents in Kamloops.  In 1987 and 1988, they travelled to Reno
together for one week each time.

After they decided to live
together in 1984, they searched for and selected new accommodation together.
The rental agreement was in both their names.  They opened a joint chequing
account and deposited their pay cheques into it.  All household expenses
including the cost of furnishings, were paid from their joint bank account.

Mr. Garneau also maintained a
savings bank account that pre-dated their relationship, but the Petitioner had
access to this account with a bank card.  Amounts deposited into this account
came from their pay cheques or their joint bank account.  This account was used
as a "rainy day fund" and for vacations.

In late 1985, Mr. Garneau was
diagnosed as having a potentially fatal condition.  The Petitioner gave serious
consideration to continuing their relationship at this time, including the risk
to his own health.  He decided to stay in the relationship with Mr. Garneau.

Mr. Garneau was unable to work
after May 27, 1988.  The petitioner maintained their household on his single
income from this time onwards.  Mr. Garneau executed a Will in the petitioner's
favour as a sole beneficiary.  Mr. Garneau died on March 17, 1989.

In June 1988, Mr. Garneau was no
longer eligible for health benefits through his employment.  The Petitioner
applied to include Mr. Garneau as his dependent spouse under his health care
plan through his employment.  The Collective Agreement between the Union and
the Hospital provides a Health Care Plan for all eligible employees, which
includes the Petitioner.

The health care plan through
the Petitioner's employment includes basic medical care coverage, as well as
dental care and extended health care benefits.  The Respondent Commission is
the carrier of the Petitioner's basic medical care coverage under the
Collective Agreement.

From 1986 to 1989, the Collective
Agreement between the Union and the Hospital defined a "Common-Law
Spouse" as,

"A man or woman not
married to each other, who have lived together as husband and wife for a period
of not less than two years."

During collective bargaining in
1989, the Collective Agreement was modified effective April 1, 1989, to add the
following definition for a "Common-Law Spouse":

"Two people who
have cohabited as spousal partners for a period of not less than two (2)
years."

The purpose of this modification
was to extend benefits available under the Health Care Plan to same-sex
spouses.

On June 21, 1988, the Union filed
a grievance on behalf of the Petitioner, pursuant to the Collective Agreement,
with respect to the denial of basic medical care benefits to Mr. Garneau.  The
Hospital responded that it had no control over the definition used by the
Respondent Commission, however, it would reimburse the petitioner for any
expenses incurred to change the definition to include same-sex relationships,
if the Petitioner was successful.

On September 1, 1988, Deborah
Nivins wrote a letter to the Union's representative on behalf of the Respondent
Commission.  In her letter, the relevant portion of which was set out above,
Ms. Nivins denied coverage to Mr. Garneau on the basis of the interpretation
placed on the definition of spouse.

On September 18, 1988, the
Hospital, in a letter to the Union's representative, stated a willingness to
pay the necessary premiums to enrol Mr. Garneau as the Petitioner's dependent
spouse provided the Commission accepted coverage for same-sex spouses. There is
no dispute that Mr. Garneau was eligible for coverage in all respects under the
Plan, but for the Commission's position that homosexual relationships were not
considered to be "spousal".

The Hospital did collect premiums
from the Petitioner for medical coverage for Mr. Garneau, and the Hospital remitted
payments for the Plan to the Commission up to March 3l, l989.

Mr. Cunningham, Director of the
Registration and Premium Billing Branch with the Commission, has deposed that
Mr. Garneau received medical coverage through the Ministry of Social Services
and Housing from November 1, 1988 to March 31, 1989.  He states that the
Commission waived the payment of the premium during this period of time.

The Petitioner has deposed that
while Mr. Garneau received Social Assistance during the periods stated in Mr.
Cunningham's Affidavit, he had to pay for very expensive medication, and that
they were never told that the premiums were waived from November 1, 1988 to
March 31, 1989.  They continued to pay the premiums to the Hospital who
remitted them to the Commission.  Mr. Knodel has deposed that knowing that the
premiums could be waived would have reduced the stress experienced by both Mr.
Garneau and himself.  There is no dispute that the Petitioner and Mr. Garneau
were unaware that the premiums were not payable.

The Psychiatric Evidence

An expert report from Dr. Michael
Myers, a Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University
of British Columbia, was included in the material before the court.  Dr. Myers
reviewed the various determinants of homosexuality in men and women in his
report dated May 9, 1991, titled "A Psychiatric Approach To
Homosexuality" ("Report").

Dr. Myers reports that
"there is a high degree of similarity between homosexual and heterosexual
life partners and that they are much more the same in their attitudes,
expectations, and values than are different."  He defines homosexuality
as,

"being attracted to
members of one's own sex, as opposed to heterosexuality which is the attraction
to members of the opposite sex.  Homosexuality can also refer to one's erotic
fantasies, thoughts, feelings, and desires, to one's sexual activity with
others; to one's sense of identity; and to one's social role."

He states that the incidence of
homosexual behaviour in Western culture is conservatively estimated as 5 to 10
percent for adult males and 3 to 5 percent for adult females.  In 1973, the
American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality as a psychiatric disease
from its diagnostic nomenclature.  This was followed by the Canadian
Psychiatric Association.  He reports that his experience and observations as a
psychiatrist indicate that notwithstanding the fact that homosexuality is no
longer deemed a form of mental or psychiatric illness, lay persons continue to
believe that there is something wrong or strange with individuals who develop
attachments to members of their own sex, and label them as "deviant and
immoral".

Dr. Myers reviewed the various
determinants of homosexual behaviour including, biological, neuroendocrine (study
of brain hormones in the fetus and its influence), genetic, gender
identity/role.  He adopts the view expressed by Dr. Margrit Eichler in
Families
in Canada Today, Recent Changes and Their Policy Consequences
, (Toronto:
Gage, 2nd. ed., l988) that the term "family" does not have one
definition for all purposes in Canada.  As families evolve in our pluralistic
society, the language by which families are described evolves.  Dr. Eichler
uses the term "familial relationship" to characterize the many kinds
of relationships that exist outside of the traditional and legally married
family.

Dr. Myers reviewed the
Petitioner's Affidavit and interviewed him on May 6, 1991.  He concluded that
the Petitioner had a familial relationship with Garneau.

"There was an
expectation of continuance.  They were deeply committed to each other
(emotionally and sexually), exchanged vows and rings in a private ceremony,
established a home together, pooled their finances, and shared bank accounts
and credit cards.  Further Mr. Knodel did not separate from or abandon Mr.
Garneau when the latter became ill.  Like a heterosexual spouse, Mr. Knodel was
named as sole beneficiary in Mr. Garneau's will; he assisted and supported his
life-partner, including nursing and comforting him, until his death March 17,
1989.  It was only after threatening a grievance charge that Mr. Knodel was
granted a few days of compassionate leave (as opposed to days deducted from his
vacation leave) from work to organize, and attend Mr. Garneau's funeral."

Dr. Myers reports that homosexual
people as a group are stigmatized in our society.  He characterized stigma as
"a mark of disgrace or infamy; a stain or reproach, as on one's
reputation; a characteristic mark or sign of defect, degeneration, or disease".
In his opinion the stigma causes psychological and related social problems.

He concludes that,

"It appears that
the strongest evidence we have thus far is biological to explain same-sex
affectionate and erotic feelings in homosexual people.  Although there seems to
be some abnormality in brain differentiation of the developing fetus during the
prenatal period, one's sense of being different does not begin until childhood,
usually before the ages of 5 and 6.  This inner sense (gender identity) or behaviour
(gender role) is usually influenced by a host of non-biological factors such as
the family and society in which one develops.  By the time of puberty, most of
these individuals, who have felt `different' as children, begin to experience
strong feelings of attraction to members of their own sex.  They have no
control over these feelings - they are not a deliberate choice.  For most of
them, this is very frightening and lonely, because they gave come to believe
that what they are experiencing is not considered normal by most of society.
This then leads to isolation, unhappiness, self-loathing, and a sense of
inferiority.  I have listened to the life stories of hundreds of homosexual men
and women and I can attest to the pervasive influence of discriminatory ideas,
beliefs, and laws on the sense of these individuals.  This indifferent or
hostile climate not only damages one's worthiness as a free and health
individual in our society but causes many people to lead double or fragmented
lives.  They dare not be open for fear of further ridicule and rejection.  Many
attempt to pass as heterosexual people and do their best to conform.  When they
meet someone else, fall in love, and become a couple, they are usually much
happier and find it easier to cope with life."

ANALYSIS

Nature of the Legislation

The
MSA
provides a
skeletal framework and establishes the institutional structure necessary for
the operation of the Plan.  The operational structure of the Plan is contained
in the
Regulations
.  The Plan, established pursuant to s. 9 of the
MSA
,
is a voluntary medical plan for the provision of medical insurance and
licensing of carriers that provide medical insurance in the Province.  The
Commission is duly authorized under s. 7 of the
MSA
to administer and
operate the Plan.  It functions as a public authority to exercise and perform
any power or duty for and on behalf of the Province: s. 3.03 of the
Regulations
.

The
Regulations
are
divided into the following relevant divisions:

Division 2: Interpretation;

Division 3: The Commission;

Division 4: The Plan;

Division 5: Payment for Services under
the Plan;

Division 6: Insured Persons under the
Plan;

Division 8: Premiums;

Division 14: Eligible Persons: Premium
Assistance Requirements.

A resident of the Province is
eligible to apply to join the Plan, that is become a subscriber and an insured
person, after living in the Province for two months (s. 6.04).  It is the
responsibility of every resident to enrol in the Plan and maintain coverage for
himself or herself and his or her dependents (s. 6.01(2)).

The premiums payable by
subscribers are fixed by the Commission.  The Plan permits employers and
employees to allocate the relative amount of premiums due to the Commission
between themselves by a collective agreement or any other arrangement (s.
8.04).

The definition of spouse in the
Regulations

was added in l977.  Before that, coverage was not available to heterosexual
common-law couples.

In s. 1 of the
Medical Services
Act
, "eligible person" is defined:

"eligible
person" means a person who satisfies the commission that he

(a)has
maintained his permanent residence in the Province for 12 consecutive months
immediately prior to his application for payment of part of a premium under
this Act;

(b)is
not principally dependent on another person as specified in the regulations or
exempt from liability to pay income tax by reason of a special status or
membership; and

(c)is
not a person

(i)for
whom medical, surgical or obstetrical care or diagnostic services are provided
under an agreement or arrangement that the care or services are paid for by the
Province other than pursuant to the
Hospital Insurance Act
; or

(ii)for
whose health and welfare care Canada is responsible;

Section 14.01 of the
Regulations

provides:

14.01
For the purposes of the definition
of "eligible person" in section 1 of the Act, a person is principally
dependant on another where the person is a dependent of a subscriber.

Under s. 2.01 of the
Regulations
,
"dependant" is is defined:

"dependant"
means a spouse or a child ordinarily resident in the Province of British
Columbia

Section 14.02 provides:

14.02
(1)  In this section
'adjusted
net income"
means the net income of the eligible person in the
immediately preceding taxation year as shown on line 236 of his income tax
return and, where the eligible person has a spouse, means the combined net
income of the eligible person and his spouse in the immediately preceding
taxation year, adjusted by making the following deductions:

(a)$3
000 for a dependant spouse;

(b)$3
000 for each of the eligible person and his spouse who has attained the age of
65 years on or before December 31 of the current taxation year;

(c)$3
000 for each dependant child minus one-half of the child care expense deduction
as shown on line 214 of his income tax return;

(d)$3
000 for each family member who had a disability during the immediately
preceding taxation year within the meaning of the
Income Tax Act

(Canada).

(2)  For
the purposes of subsection (1),
"dependant"
means a person who
receives coverage under the plan as the result of being listed with the plan as
a dependant of the eligible person.

(3)  Subject
to section 14.03, the percentage of premium payable by an eligible person is

(a)5%
where the adjusted net income does not exceed $9 000,

(b)25%
where the adjusted net income exceeds $9 000 but does not exceed $11 000,

(c)45%
where the adjusted net income exceeds $11 000 but does not exceed $13 000,

(d)65%
where the adjusted net income exceeds $13 000 but does not exceed $15 000,

(e)85%
where the adjusted net income exceeds $15 000 but does not exceed $17 000, or

(f)100%
where the adjusted net income exceeds $17 000.

The definition of
"spouse" in s.2.0l of the
Regulations
permits both legally
married couples and common-law heterosexual couples to claim their respective
spouses as "dependants" under the Plan.  Under the current schedule,
a subscriber without any dependants and who does not qualify for premium
assistance pays $372.00 per year.  Two separate subscribers would therefore pay
$744.00 per year ($372.00 x 2).  However, the same subscriber with one
"dependant" whether a "spouse" or a "child", pays
$660.00 per year.  Therefore, assuming no qualification for premium assistance
the present effect of excluding same-sex couples from the definition of the
word "spouse" results in an annual premium which is $84.00 (or l3%)
more than that paid by heterosexual couples.

Two subscribers, who, for example,
are each qualified for 95% premium assistance, would separately pay $l8.60
annually, or a total of $37.20 annually.  A dependant discount for a subscriber
with one dependant would reduce his or her annual premium from $37.20 to
$33.00, a saving of $4.20 per year.

Dental and Extended Health Care
Benefits under Collective Agreements

Benefits have been extended to
same sex spouses, not under the legislation, but under collective agreements
which provide for dental and extended care benefits.

Robert Bucher, General Manager
and CEO of the CU&C Health Services Society ("CU&C"), has
deposed that CU&C provides group dental, extended health and weekly
indemnity benefits for approximately 250,000 members in British Columbia.
These members are employed by both private sector and public sector employers.
The coverage under their plan is extended to the spouses and the dependants of
the members bringing the total number of individuals covered to approximately
600,000 persons.

Mr. Bucher has further deposed
that CU&C has 7 group contracts covering 1,700 members where the benefits
are provided to same-sex partners.  Further, CU&C has received instructions
from other employers representing 18,000 members to provide coverage to
same-sex partners, notwithstanding the restrictive definition in their
contract.  He has also deposed that CU&C is confident that it will be able
to provide coverage to same-sex spouses with no increase in actuarial risk.

Wayne Kemmett, Vice President of
the Medical Services Association ("MSA"), has deposed that MSA
provides group health benefits to over one million members in British
Columbia.  These benefits are extended to the members' spouses and dependants.
The benefits include extended health, dental, wage indemnity, life, long term
disability, and accidental death and dismemberment insurance.   Within the past
two years, MSA has provided same-sex benefits for some employers representing
20,000 members in the Province.

Is the issue of discrimination
academic in this case
?

The Medical Services Plan is
funded, in part, from premium payments made by subscribers.  Premiums are fixed
from time to time by the Commission in a "Schedule of Premium
Payments".

The amount of the premiums is a
function of a subscriber's income and the number of his dependants.

As to income, under the premium
schedule that was in effect from May l, l988 to June 30, l989, a subscriber
qualified for premium assistance if his or her annual taxable income was below
a specified level:  95% assistance for income below $2,500;  55% assistance for
income between $2,500 to $6,500;  no assistance if income above $6,500.

The schedule which came into
effect on July l, l989, provided for premium assistance as follows:  l5% for
l988 adjusted net income between $l5,000 and $l7,000,  35% for income between
$l3,000 and $l5,000,  65% for income between $ll,000 and $l3,000,  75% for
income between $9,000 and $ll,000 and 95% if income is $9,000 or less.

In this case, Mr. Garneau became
unable to work after June l988, but in l988, Mr. Garneau's taxable income was
$l4,8l7.l0, which is above the level at which premium assistance was provided.
In l987, his income had been $24,2l5.05.  In l988, there was no premium
assistance to a subscriber whose net income was above $6,500.

Although in principle the
legislative scheme provides premium assistance to those who have income below a
certain level, Mr. Garneau's income in l987 and l988 excluded the availability
of premium assistance.

As of November l988, Mr. Garneau
began to receive social assistance.  Although at that point, medical premium
payments under s.8.07 of the
Regulations
became payable by the agency
responsible for his medical care, that was not known to either Mr. Garneau or
the Petitioner.  The Hospital submitted the premiums to the Commission for Mr.
Garneau at a single subscriber rate up to the time of his death in March l989,
and the Commission received the premium payments.

In paragraph l3 of his affidavit,
Mr. Dan Cunningham, the Director of the Registration and Premium Billing Branch
of the Medical Services Commission deposed:

l3.  The records of the
Medical Services Plan show that in the case of Mr. Garneau for the period of
November l, l988 to March 2l, l989, the Medical Services Plan waived payment by
Mr. Garneau of any part of the Medical Services Plan premium insofar as he was
in receipt of medical coverage from the Ministry of Social Services and Housing
during that time.

How the Commission could have
both waived and collected premiums for Mr. Garneau is unexplained, but it is in
any event irrelevant to the question of whether or not the
Regulations

discriminated against the Petitioner, for it is the operation of the
Regulations

which must be considered.

Respondent's counsel submitted
that it is not open to the Petitioner to attack legislation in the abstract,
and referred to
Re. Allen and the Superintendent of Motor Vehicles et al

(l986) 27 C.C.C. (3d) 5l9 (B.C.S.C.) in support of his submission.  At least in
the period between June and November l988, when the former premium schedule
applied, the issue raised by the Petitioner is not academic.  This is not a
case of hypothetical disadvantage.

Moreover, there exists a
"live controversy".   It is of sufficient import to justify the
court's use of its discretionary power to issue a declaration in accordance
with the test in
Borowski
v.
Attorney-General
of Canada
,
1989 CanLII 123 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 342  (S.C.C.)
.

The Petitioner's claim and the issues
raised by it

The Petitioner's position is that
the effect of the
Regulations
is to discriminate against him solely on
the basis of his sexual orientation by denying the equal benefit of the law
available to heterosexual spouses.  The
Regulations
have a further
impact of adversely effecting his dignity and self-esteem and perpetuate the
"homophobia" expressed by members in society.

The first issue is whether or not
the definition of spouse in s.2.0l of the
Regulations
may be interpreted
to include two persons living together in a homosexual relationship.

The second issue, if the
definition of spouse is interpreted so as not to include same-sex couples, is
whether or not the Petitioner's right to equality under s.l5(l) of the
Charter

has been infringed by the denial of coverage to same-sex couples?

The third issue, if there is an
infringement of the Petitioner's s.l5(l) right, is whether or not the
infringement is demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society under
s.l of the
Charter
.  Although the Respondent's counsel conceded that if
there was an infringement, it could not be justified under s.l, I have set out
the third issue for convenience, because some of the submissions made appeared
to me to fall into a Section l argument, rather than addressing the
infringement issue.

The fourth issue is,

(5)If
the s.l5(l) infringement is not saved by s.l of the
Charter
, what is the
just and appropriate remedy in the circumstances?

(a)Should
granting of coverage to same-sex couples be read-in to the definition of
"spouse" in the
Regulations
, or,

(b)Should
the definition of "spouse" in the
Regulations
be struck out
and held to be of no force or effect?

Grounds of Descrimination

Section 15(1)
of the
Charter

lists nine enumerated grounds of discrimination.  These are: race, national or
ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

The listed ground that seems most
applicable is "sex".  Therefore, the question is whether sexual
orientation is included in the term "sex" in
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
?

In
Janzen
v.
Platy Ent. Ltd.
.

1989 CanLII 97 (SCC)
,
[1989] 4 W.W.R. 39
, the Supreme Court of Canada considered meaning of discrimination
on the basis of sex.  In this case, the court held that sexual harassment in
the workplace fell within the definition of discrimination on the basis of
sex.  Whilst the court was concerned with treatment in the workplace, Dickson
C.J.C. stated on behalf of the Court at p. 61:

"... discrimination
on the basis of sex may be defined as practices or attitudes which have the
effect of limiting the conditions of employment of, or the employment
opportunities available to, employees on the
basis of a characteristic
related to gender
." [emphasis is mine].

In the present case, the effect
of the legislation is not aimed at a characteristic related to gender.  The
definition of "spouse" that is challenged effects both men and women
who are engaged in a homosexual relationship.  Further, there is no indication
that the discriminatory effects fall entirely on men as in
Brooks
v.
Canada Safeway Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 96 (SCC)
,

The definition of spouse

For convenience, I will again set
out the definition of "spouse" as it appears in the
Regulations
.

"spouse"
includes a man or woman who, not being married to each other, live together as
man and wife.

On behalf of the Petitioner, Mr.
Steeves submitted that the definition is ambiguous. The subject for the phrase
"live together as husband and wife" is "man or woman" but
the use of "or" is inappropriate.  Substituting "and" for
"or" addresses the problem but it is not consistent with spouse in
the singular.

Further he submitted, the use of
the word "includes" clearly indicates that the definition is not exhaustive.
In Mr. Steeves submission, the definition does not expressly or necessarily
exclude same-sex spouses, and an interpretation of "spouse" that is
consistent with the
Charter
permits the inclusion of same-sex partners
in the definition.

Where a statutory term is said to
conflict with the provisions of the
Charter
, then the constitutional
validity of that term must be put in issue for the
Charter
to play a
role in resolving the dispute and, in this case, the definition of spouse
contained in the
Regulations
has been put in issue.

Respondents' counsel submitted
that the definition of "spouse" in the
Regulations
, although
not well drafted, clearly was intended to cover married and common law
heterosexual couples.  The definition, he argued, does not make a distinction
based upon sexual orientation but is simply a distinction between
"spouses" and "non-spouses".  In his submission, a same-sex
couple is not treated any differently from any other adult couple whose members
do not hold themselves out as man and wife but share a household.

Implicit in the Respondents'
position is the assumption that a homosexual couple cannot be
"spouses".

Mr. Pearlman, on behalf of the
Respondent, also submitted that a homosexual couple, neither of whom qualifies
for any income assistance, has an advantage which a heterosexual couple does
not have.  The example he gave for illustrative purposes was that of a
homosexual couple where the income of one falls to the point of qualifying for
benefits of premium rate assistance.  He submitted that that benefit was never
extended to heterosexual couples, and where the income of one spouse is reduced
to 0, if the other spouse continues to earn net adjusted annual income of
$l7,000 or more, the premium will still be $660 per annum since, in effect, the
income of one spouse is pooled with the other.  Thus, he argued, the fact that
the Plan does not pool income is often an advantage for same-sex couples.  The
reference to pooling of income comes from s.l4.02 of the
Regulations
which
defines "adjusted net income".  Section 14.02 has been set out
earlier in the judgment.

To analyze whether or not the
impact of including same-sex couples in the definition of spouse would result
in a detriment in some instances and a benefit in others is not a useful
exercise in this case.  There is a dependant discount which is unavailable to
same-sex couples, assuming the definition of spouse is interpreted to include
only heterosexual spouses, but if the definition of "spouse" includes
same-sex spouses, the income pooling between spouses which is required under
s.l4.02 of the
Regulations
for the purposes of determining premium
assistance would also apply.  From an examination of the
Act
and
Regulations
,
it seems clear that the legislation does provide a benefit to married and
common-law heterosexual couples, and that is a benefit from which same-sex
couples are presently excluded.

There is no dispute that the term
"spouse" is intended to include legally married couples.  The
addition of the phrase "includes a man or woman who, not being married to
each other", is clearly intended to include common-law couples.  This is
evident from the use of the words "to each other".

The remainder of the phrase
requires the couple to "live together as husband and wife".  This
phrase is intended to exclude other types of relationships such as the type
that exists between, for example, siblings or between other adult persons who
live together but who do not share an emotional and sexual commitment.

However, this phrase does not
require a couple
to be husband and wife
.  It is not intended to import a
traditional role for a husband or a wife.  Nor is it intended for each partner
in the relationship to adopt the role of either a "husband" or a
"wife".  The use of the word "as" suggests a particular
type of relationship that involves both emotional and sexual aspects.

In the present case, the evidence
is overwhelming that the Petitioner and Mr. Garneau lived "as husband and
wife".  There was an expectation of continuance.  They were deeply
committed to each other emotionally and sexually, exchanged vows and rings in a
private ceremony, established a home together, pooled their finances, and
shared bank accounts and credit cards.  The Petitioner did not separate from or
abandon Mr. Garneau when the latter became ill, notwithstanding the risk to
him.  Like a heterosexual spouse, the Petitioner was named as sole beneficiary
in Mr. Garneau's will;  he assisted and supported his life-partner, including
nursing and comforting him, until his death March l7, l989.  The evidence of
Dr. Myers also suggests that the type of emotional bond between homosexual
couples is no different than one between heterosexual couples.

In the present case, two phrases

The definition in the

begins "spouse includes ..."

With respect to the meaning of the
word "spouse", it is clear that absent any infringement of a specific

legally married couples.  This is not a case where there are two different or
ambiguous interpretations.  Where the statutory or legislative provision leads

With respect to the phrase

does not
dictate that the term "spouse" must, as a matter of law, include in
all circumstances all legally married and common-law couples who are homosexual

(a)
Scope of s. 15(1) of the
Charter

Section 15(1)
of the
Charter

reads,

"15.(1)Every
individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal
protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in
particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability."

In
Andrews
v.
Law Society of
British Columbia
,
1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 143
,
56 D.L.R. (4th) 1
, the Supreme Court
of Canada held that
s.15(1)
of the
Charter
was not a general guarantee
of equality.  At page 171 (p. 15 D.L.R.), McIntyre J. stated the purpose of
s.
15
(this view was endorsed by all the members of the court):

"It is clear that
the purpose of
s. 15
is to ensure equality in the formulation and application
of the law.  The promotion of equality entails the promotion of a society in
which all are secure in the knowledge that they are recognized at law as human
beings equally deserving of concern, respect and consideration.  It has a large
remedial component."

McIntyre J. defined a two-step
process for application of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
at page 182 (pp.
23-24 D.L.R.) as follows"

"A complainant
under s. 15(1) must show not only that he or she is not receiving equal
treatment before and under the law or that the law has a differential impact on
him or her in the protection or benefit accorded by law but, in addition, must
show that the legislative impact of the law is discriminatory".

And at page 174 McIntyre J.
defined discrimination as follows:

"I would say then
that discrimination may be described as a distinction, whether intentional or
not but based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of the individual
or group, which has the effect of imposing burdens, obligations, or
disadvantages on such individual or group not imposed upon others, or which
withholds or limits access to opportunities, benefits, and advantages available
to other members of the society.  Distinctions based on personal
characteristics attributed to an individual solely on the basis of association
with a group will rarely escape the charge of discrimination, while those based
on an individual's merits and capacities will rarely be so classified.

...

In general, it may be
said that the principles which have been applied under the Human Rights Acts
are equally applicable in considering questions of discrimination under s.
15(1)."

The Supreme Court also concluded
that groups forming "discrete and insular minorities" as described in

United States
v.
Carolene
Products Co.
, 304 U.S. 144 at pp. 152-3, n.4, 82 L. Ed. 1234 (1938) were
also protected by
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.  Wilson J. on behalf of the
majority, defined such groups at page 152 as,

"I emphasize,
moreover, that this is a determination which is not to be made only in the
context of the law which is subject to challenge but rather in the context of
the place of the group in the entire social, political and legal fabric of our
society.  While legislatures must inevitably draw distinctions among the
governed, such distinctions should not bring about or reinforce the disadvantage
of certain groups and individuals by denying them the rights freely accorded to
others."

The next case involving
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
at the Supreme Court of Canada involved a challenge by

v.
The Queen
,

1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 1296  (S.C.C.)

With respect to

(c)
Application of s. 15(1) of the

Charter
to the facts at bar

The rights defined in
s. 15
of
the
Charter
are stated to be applicable to "every
individual".  The rights enumerated in this section signify rights
according human dignity.  The respect for the individual person means respect
for the unique and diverse character of every human person.  This implies a
large degree of tolerance within a pluralistic society.  Discrimination is
abhorrent because it treats individuals as abstractions rather than as
individuals.  Personal qualities are lost in the group stereotype.

The applicable test under
s.
15(1)
of the
Charter
may be stated as follows:

(1)Does
the petitioner's claim disclose unequal treatment?

(2)If
so, is the impact of this treatment discriminatory?

This
involves an inquiry into the following:

i.Does
the legislation make a distinction based on enumerated grounds listed in s.
15(1)?

ii.If
not, is the distinction based on un-enumerated grounds which fall within the
ambit of s. 15(1)?

iii.Does
this distinction impose a burden on the petitioner?

iv.Is
the distinction based on individual merit and capacity?

v.If
the distinction is based upon membership within an identifiable group or class
in society, does this group constitute a discrete and insular minority within
society?  What is the context of this group within society.

vi.Is
this distinction a necessary departure from the principle of universal
application of the law?

The answer must be in the
affirmative for the following items: (i) or (ii), (iii), and (v); and in the
negative for items (iv) and (vi) to show an infringement of the Petitioner's
rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

(l)
Does
the petitioner's claim disclose unequal treatment?

Preliminary examination of the
Regulations

and
MSA
indicate that the definition of "spouse" in s. 2.01 of
the
Regulations
, has the effect of treating homosexual couples
differently than to heterosexual couples.  This difference in treatment is not
readily explainable or related to the purpose of the legislation.  Accordingly,
the petitioner has satisfied the threshold test of demonstrating unequal
treatment.

(2)
If
so, is the impact of this treatment discriminatory?

i.
Does this distinction impose a
burden on the petitioner?

In the present case, the
legislative provision is attacked not because it subjects the individuals
covered by it to discriminatory effect, but rather because it
excludes

individuals solely because of their sexual orientation.

The petitioner deposes that
because the
MSA
and the
Regulations
makes a distinction on the
basis of sexual orientation, it exacerbates conditions of disadvantage.  The
evidence of Dr. Myers indicates the "pervasive influence of discriminatory
ideas, beliefs, and laws on the sense of these individuals."  In his view,
this indifferent or hostile climate damages one's worthiness as a free and
healthy individual in our society.  However, these problems are lessened when
they (homosexual individuals) "meet someone else, fall in love, and become
a couple."

Additionally, the legislation
does impose an economic penalty on homosexual couples relative to heterosexual
couples who live together in a relationship akin to man and wife, by denying a
benefit available to heterosexual couples.

The Respondents say that any
burden that is imposed upon the petitioner is minimal or insubstantial, and the
Court ought to be reluctant to restrict the operating latitude of the
Legislature. However, once a burden is imposed on a person alleging a s. 15(1)
infringement, the relative weighing of the interests of the Legislature against
the rights of the petitioner is properly handled under
s. 1
of the
Charter
,
and not at this stage.

Under-Inclusion

In
Brooks
v.
Canada Safeway
Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 96 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 1219  (S.C.C.)
, the respondent's group insurance plan
provided weekly benefits for loss of pay due to sickness or illness.  The
insurance plan covered pregnant employees but excluded coverage during the
period commencing the tenth week prior to the expected week of confinement and
ending with the sixth week after the week of confinement.  The appellants filed
complaints with the Manitoba Human Rights Commission alleging that
discrimination on the basis of pregnancy constituted discrimination on the
basis of sex.  The claims were dismissed by the adjudicator, the Court of
Queen's Bench and the Court of Appeal.

The Supreme Court of Canada in a
unanimous decision by Dickson C.J., allowed the appeal.  Notwithstanding that
the respondent had no intention to discriminate, Dickson C.J. stated at p.
1239:

"Intent to
discriminate is not a necessary element of discrimination."

With respect to the argument that
the insurance "plan is not discriminatory but merely underinclusive of the
potential risks it could conceivably insure", Dickson C.J. stated at p.
1240:

"Underinclusion may
be simply a backhanded way of permitting discrimination.  Increasingly,
employee benefit plans have become part of the terms and conditions of
employment.  Once an employer decides to provide an employee benefit package,
exclusions from such schemes may not be made in a discriminatory fashion."

In
Brown
v.
B.C.
(l990),
42
B.C.L.R. 294 (B.C.S.C.)
Coultas J. cited with approval the first sentence above
and stated that this principle was applicable in a
Charter
context.  At
p. 313, he stated:

"
Brooks
was
not a
Charter
case.  However in
Andrews
v.
Law Society of B.C.
,
supra, Mr. Justice McIntyre considered the application of principles applied in
human rights cases to those cases invoking the Charter."

Where the State makes a
distinction between two classes of individuals, A and B, that has the effect of
imposing a greater burden on individuals within class B, and if the individuals
within class B fall within the class of individuals protected by
s. 15(1)
of
the
Charter
, the manner in which the legislative provision or law is
drafted is irrelevant for constitutional purposes; ie., it is immaterial
whether the subject law states: (1) A benefits; or (2) Everyone benefits except
B.  In both cases, the impact upon the individual within group B is the same.

The state is not required to
remedy all aspects of a particular mischief or none at all.  The state in the
regulation of the economy and taxing of its subjects is free to remedy parts of
a mischief or to recognize degrees of evil and to strike at the harm where it
thinks it most acute.

However, it does not follow that
a burden imposed on an individual solely on the basis of his or her sexual
orientation is constitutionally permissible.  When the impact of the law is
discriminatory, it matters little whether the discrimination is intentional or
a necessary consequence of the law.  Normally it is considered proper that the
State distinguish between individuals only on the basis of their ability or
need.

Such a distinction is valid only
if the purpose of the law rationally supports such a distinction.  This exercise
is properly considered under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.  This will generally
require a consideration by the Court of the "evil" to be remedied by
the law.  A constitutionally impermissible purpose will not save the law under
s. 1 of the
Charter
:
R.
v.
Big M Drug Mart
.

The distinction should not be
illusory, arbitrary or invidious.  In cases where the law makes a distinction
based on a prohibited ground of discrimination under either the Human Rights
Codes or the
Charter
it will be necessary that the State demonstrate an
overriding justification for the use of such distinction and show that the
purpose of the action could not be accomplished by a non-discriminatory focused
alternative.

Accordingly, I have concluded
that underinclusion on the basis of a discriminatory ground, such as sexual
orientation, is also prohibited by the
Charter
.

ii.
Is
the distinction based on individual merit and capacity?

In the present case, it is clear
that the distinction is not related to the petitioner's merit or capacity.

iii.
If
the distinction is based upon membership within an identifiable group or class
in society, does this group constitute a discrete and insular minority within
society?

In
Brown
v.
B.C.
,
supra
,
Coultas J. stated at p. 309:

"The history of
western civilization records that from biblical times to our own, homosexuals
have been subjected to discrimination because of their sexual orientation.  As
with other forms of discrimination, it is unjust for it fails to take into
account individual merit, character or accomplishment.  The form and extent of
it is uglier, the cry more shrill since the onset of AIDS."

T.C. Van Boven,
Distinguishing
Criteria of Human Rights
, in Vasak, Karl (ed.)
The International
Dimensions of Human Rights
, (l982), Vol. l, pp. 48-56 noted that generally
a group may be taken as a collectivity of persons who have special and distinct
characteristics, who find themselves in specific situations or conditions.
Those special and distinct conditions may be of a racial, ethnological,
national, linguistic or religious nature.  The specific situations or
conditions could be determined by political, economic, social or cultural
factors.  Taking into account these characteristics that are inherent in the
group, human rights law including the
Charter
, aims at protecting and
preserving these characteristics or aims at bringing about changes in the
conditions or situations affecting the group which are intolerable under the
law.

In the present case, the evidence
of Dr. Myers confirms that

"homosexual people as a group are
stigmatized in our society."  The petitioner falls within the group that
constitutes a "discrete and insular minority" within the meaning of

s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

iv.
Is
this distinction a necessary departure from the principle of universal
application of the law?

In
MacKay
v.
R.

(1980),
1980 CanLII 217 (SCC)
,
114
D.L.R. (3d) 393  (S.C.C.)
, McIntyre J. offered a broad definition of
"equality before the law" by stating at p. 423:

"whether an
inequality has been created for a valid federal constitutional objective ...
and whether it is a necessary departure from the general principle of universal
application of the law for the attainment of some necessary and desirable
social objective."

In the present case, a
consideration involving the "departure from the general principle of
universal application of the law" belongs under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

Democracy professes to provide
fair access and to give fair consideration to the views, needs and claims of
all persons within society.  The purpose of s. 15(1) is to ensure that
individuals falling within its ambit may participate fully in society.
Therefore, when the government takes on an obligation and provides a benefit,
s. 15(1) makes denial of that benefit to other groups questionable.

While not all instances of
under-inclusion infringe
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, whenever the
government confers a benefit, any conditions to the receipt of the benefit must
pass constitutional muster:
Professional Institute of the
Public Service of Canada
v.
Commissioner of the Northwest Territories et
al.; Attorney General of Canada et al., Interveners
(l990), 72 D.L.R. (4th)
l Sopinka J. at p. 19  (S.C.C.).

In the present case, I have
concluded that the petitioner has met the burden of demonstrating that the
exclusion of homosexual couples from the definition of "spouse" in
2.01 of the
Regulations
, is discriminatory within the meaning of
s.
15(1)
of the
Charter
.

Section 1
of the
Charter

In the present proceedings, the
Respondents' counsel conceded that if the definition of "spouse" in
the
Regulations
infringes
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, it could not
be justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

Section 24(1)
of the
Charter

(a)Interpretation

Section 24(1)
of the
Charter

provides:

"24. (1)  Anyone
whose rights or freedoms, as guaranteed by this
Charter
, have been infringed or
denied may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction to obtain such remedy as
the court considers appropriate and just in the circumstances."

This provision incorporates two
basic purposes.  First, it serves to provide standing to litigants who allege a
violation of their
Charter
rights and freedoms:
Operation Dismantle
v.
The
Queen

(1985),
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
,
18 D.L.R. (4th) 481  (S.C.C.)
.  Second, it serves as a
remedial provision to permit a "court of competent jurisdiction" the
power to grant a remedy that it "considers appropriate and just in the
circumstances".  A Superior Court is court of competent jurisdiction:
R.
v.
Mills
,
1986 CanLII 17 (SCC)
,
[1986] 1
S.C.R. 863  (S.C.C.)
.

Section 24(1) is not the
exclusive source of remedies for
Charter
contravention.  It has been
held that s. 24(1) grants additional remedial authority to remedy
Charter

violations:
R.
v.
Erickson

(1984),

1984 CanLII 795 (BC CA)
,
13 C.C.C. (3d) 269
at 273,
per Esson J.A.  (B.C.C.A.).  Nothing in the
Charter

serves to limit or restrict the inherent powers of a superior court to fashion
a just and appropriate remedy in the circumstances.

Wilson J. speaking for the
majority
in
Gamble
v.
The Queen
,

1988 CanLII 15 (SCC)
,
[1988] 2 S.C.R. 595  (S.C.C.)
at p. 638,
emphasized the need for flexibility in
the granting of remedies:

"In general,
applicants for
Charter
relief should, I believe, be allowed a reasonable
measure of flexibility in framing their claims for relief in light of the
interests the
Charter
rights on which they rely were designed to
protect.

...

[The applicant] should
be allowed ... to seek the relief that she believes best suited to the
vindication of her rights."

(b)
Reading In and Striking Out

As stated previously, once a
person has demonstrated that a particular law infringes his or her
Charter

rights, the manner in which the law is drafted or stated ought to be irrelevant
for the purposes of a constitutional remedy.  To hold otherwise would result in
a statutory provision dictating the interpretation of the Constitution.   Further,
where B's
Charter
right to a benefit is demonstrated, it is immaterial
whether the subject law states: (1) A benefits; or (2) Everyone benefits except
B.

The first example would require
the court to "read in" the words "and B", while the second
example would require the court to "strike out" the words
"except B".  In each case, the result would be identical.

Accordingly, whether a court
"reads in" or "strikes out" words from a challenged law,
the focus of the court should be on the appropriate remedy in the circumstances
and not on the label used to arrive at the result.

(c)
Remedial Options

Section 24(1)
of the
Charter

requires the Court to fashion a remedy which is "appropriate and just in
the circumstances".  This choice is dictated primarily by the nature of
the right infringed.  In the present case, a particularly important
Charter

right is infringed, a right that the Supreme Court of Canada in
Andrews

has recognized as having "large remedial component".

The following remedial choices
appear to be open to the court in the present instance.

(i)Striking
down

The court could declare that the
definition of "spouse" in s. 2.01 of the
Regulations
is
"of no force and effect" pursuant to
s. 52(1)
of the
Charter
.
The effect of such an order would be to declare an otherwise constitutionally
valid provision invalid.  This would result in the denial of benefits to other
persons.

In
Re Phillips and Lynch et al.

(1986),
1986 CanLII 3923 (NS SC)
,
27 D.L.R. (4th) 156  (N.S.S.C.T.D.)
, an able-bodied single father
challenged the provisions for the granting of family benefits to parents in
need.  While the provisions granted benefits to single mothers, they did not
extend to single fathers.

Nunn J. found a violation of
s.
15(1)
of the
Charter
and declared that the legislation contravened the
Charter
,
however, he refused the grant an order of
certiorari
requiring the
authorities to extend the benefits to the father.  He stated at p. 159:

"Turning now to
remedy.  The remedy in this case was a rather difficult consideration.  The
court is reluctant to assume the role of legislator and while I have been asked
to amend the legislation by either reading up the word `mother' in section 5(4)
to mean parent, or by removing the words `who is disabled' from section 5(2), I
can only indicate that I am unwilling to do this.  The court ought not to
assume the role of legislator except in unique and unusual circumstances, and
then only rarely.  I feel that the only appropriate remedy to apply is to grant
a declaration that section 5(4) of the
Family Benefits Act
is of no
force or effect as it is contrary to
section 15(1)
of the
Charter
."

With deference, the remedy
referred to was not the only option open to the court.  Nunn J. invoked
s.
52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, to strike the entire legislative
provision without consideration of the flexible options under
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
.

Section 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, states that "any law that is inconsistent with the
provisions of the Constitution is,
to the extent of the inconsistency
,
of no force or effect".  As I read
s. 52(1)
, it does not require that a
validly enacted provision that benefits persons that the legislature intended
to benefit must be struck down.

In this case, striking down the
definition of "spouse" contained in the
Regulations
would go
beyond eliminating the inconsistency.

(ii) Declaration of entitlement to the
same benefit

An example of this type of remedy
is found in the decision of Strayer J.
in
Schachter
v.
Canada

(1988),
1988 CanLII 9382 (FC)
,
52 D.L.R. (4th) 525  (F.C.T.D.)
.  Strayer J. held that the failure to
provide child care related benefits to biological parents which were available
to adoptive parents under s. 32 of
Unemployment Insurance Act
, violated
the s. 15(1) guarantee of equality without discrimination based on
"sex" because that failure had "its roots in sexual stereotyping
of the respective roles of the father and mother generally" (at p. 539).

With respective to remedies,
Strayer J. stated at p. 548:

"Section 32 [of the

Unemployment Insurance Act
] is defective, not because the benefits it
provides are prohibited by the
Charter
, but rather because neither it nor any
part of the Act goes far enough in equally providing benefits to other
similarly situated, that is `under-inclusive'.  I would not consider it
`appropriate and just in the circumstances' to deprive those persons qualified
under s. 32 of their benefits.  I doubt that such an approach is `appropriate
and just' in any case involving under-inclusive provisions for social services
or income insurance:
Califano
case,
supra
[
Califano
v.
Westcott
,
443 U.S. 76, (1979)]; but
cf.

A.-G. N.S.
v.
Phillips

(1986),
1986 CanLII 3941 (NS SC)
,
34 D.L.R. (4th) 633
,
76 N.S.R. (2d) 240
,
26 C.R.R. 332 (N.S.C.A.)
.
Instead I consider it appropriate and just to make a declaration as to the
entitlement of others to the same benefits and leave it to Parliament to remedy
the situation in accordance with the Charter, either by extending similar
benefits to natural parents, or by eliminating the benefits given to adoptive
parents, or by some provision of more limited benefits on an equal basis to
both adoptive and natural parents in respect of child care.  I am not, in
effect, telling Parliament that it must follow one route or the other; all I am
determining is that if it is going to provide such benefits it must provide
them on a non-discriminatory basis.  I am prepared to assume at this stage that
Parliament will take necessary action to render equal a system of benefits
found by this court to be unequal: see
Re Hoogbruin and A.-G. B.C.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 335 (BC CA)
,
24 D.L.R. (4th) 718
,
[1986] 2 W.W.R. 700
,
70 B.C.L.R. 1
(B.C.C.A.)
."

On appeal, the Federal government
accepted the trial decision that the underinclusive provision was
discriminatory, but argued that the proper interpretation of
section 52
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, and
sections 24
and
15
of the
Charter
, required the trial
judge to declare the provision of child care benefits to be of no force and
effect.  The majority of the Federal Court of Appeal (Heald & Stone JJ.A.,
Mahoney J.A. dissenting), dismissed the appeal:
Schachter
v.
Canada

(1990),
1990 CanLII 7989 (FCA)
,
66 D.L.R. (4th) 635  (Fed. C.A.)
.  The respondents argued that
since both
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, and
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter

are triggered by a breach of the
Charter
, the court is compelled to
declare that the legislation is of no force and effect pursuant to
s. 52(1)
in
all such cases (at pp. 642).  Heald J.A., speaking for the majority, stated that
"because of the under-inclusive character of the legislation,
s. 52
cannot
apply."  Heald J.A. further stated that the positive right guaranteed by

s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, required a positive remedy (at p. 644).  He
also stated that "it would otherwise be arbitrary and capricious to have
such great substantive differences turn solely on stylistic differences in
drafting" (at p. 647).  He concluded that the court's jurisdiction under
s. 24 of the
Charter
permitted it to grant positive remedies to fit the circumstances
as they had done previously (at pp. 647-8).  Mahoney J.A. in dissent was of the
view that s. 24(1) of the
Charter
did not authorize the court to grant a
remedy that "appropriates moneys from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for a
purpose not authorized by Parliament. (at p. 661).

Leave was granted to appeal this
decision to the Supreme Court of Canada in November 1990.

The approach followed by the
trial judge in
Schachter
, and the reasons of Heald J.A. on appeal are
helpful in respect to the case at bar, although in my view,
section 52(1)
of
the
Constitution Act, 1982
, may be triggered even where the issue is
underinclusion, but the fact that s. 52(1) of the
Constitution Act, 1982
,
is triggered does not mandate or compel the court to strike the legislation in
each case.

In the present case,
s. 52(1)

while triggered, should not be used to strike the legislative provision because
it is not unconstitutional to provide benefits to married spouses and
common-law heterosexual couples.

(iii)
Declaration to include
same-sex partners

This option involves a
declaration that the definition of "spouse" in s. 2.01 of the
Regulations

includes same-sex couples.

Active judicial intervention may
be appropriate when a distinction is likely to stigmatize or perpetuate
discrimination as in this case.  In such circumstances, it is important to
consider whether it is more intrusive to strike the legislation or "read
in" the benefits to the excluded class.  In the present case, it would
clearly be far more intrusive to strike the legislation and deny the benefits
to the individuals receiving them, than it would be to extend the benefits to
the small minority who demonstrated their entitlement to them.

The Medical Services Plan is
presently available to all residents of the Province.  A declaration would not
have the effect of adding anyone to the Plan who had not previously been
eligible for coverage.

Taking into account the nature of
the breach in the context of the specific legislation under consideration,
along with the remedial aspect of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, I have
concluded that in this case a declaration that same-sex couples are included in
the definition of spouse in s. 2.01 of the
Medical Services Act Regulations

is the just and appropriate remedy.

.The

does not include two persons living in a homosexual relationship.

2
.The
petitioner's right to equality under

of the

is

.No
evidence for justification of the infringement of the s.l5(l)

of the

.

remedy that is "appropriate and just in the circumstances" within the

of the

is a declaration that same sex

to the
